name: Lena Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What happens on a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage seven people who adapt care labels and product instructions for a large outdoor-clothing company. I check that a translated washing warning still means the same thing, match labels to actual fabric and settle queries from suppliers. I’ve managed this team for seven years and do the work about as well as the other managers. I like finding one small word that would have ruined a whole batch; I hate when a launch date gives us no time to check the stitched label.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and what would a lost month of pay mean?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband, Leo, cooks at a school, and our children are seven and thirteen. We have a mortgage and about three weeks of expenses saved; my salary is low for this management job and there are few similar firms nearby. I have a bachelor’s degree and use AI now and then for a first plain-language version, but only after a colleague shows it handled an old label properly. I also mend hems for family at home, though I have never charged for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a quick draft is useful, but someone must compare the final label with the actual jacket. A wrong wash symbol can turn a good coat into a complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job should continue, which is a relief. Leo’s school kitchen closes for breaks and three weeks saved will not cover a long gap, so our mortgage still feels close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep our Wednesday fabric-and-label check and let AI suggest only the first plain-language draft after a colleague verifies the source. In the first year we’d cancel one monthly meal out and hold the 35 for school uniforms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills, even if the translation desk remains. A school break can eat those three weeks quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What label mistake stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A raincoat care card once said tumble dry when the fabric needed air drying. We stopped the print before it reached the shop, but I still remember the boxes sitting there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep using a tool you only sometimes trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a rough start on a plain sentence. The label on the real coat, not the draft, is what the customer lives with.

say: I’d compare each **final label** with the actual garment.
A quick draft cannot excuse a **wrong wash symbol**.
think: My **desk job** continues in a plateau, so I can keep paying my share of the mortgage.
Leo’s school breaks and **three-week reserve** still squeeze our household budget.
do: Keep the **Wednesday label check** and use only verified AI first drafts.
Cancel one **monthly meal out** to free 35 for uniforms.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills during school breaks.
S0.quote: The label on the real coat, not the draft, is what the customer lives with.
fieldNote: She uses AI **occasionally**, after a colleague checks old examples.
The mortgage remains tight during **school kitchen breaks**.
A specific **35 monthly cut** pays for uniforms.

steps.text: Keep Wednesday fabric-and-label checks with verified first drafts
Cancel one meal out monthly to free 35 for school uniforms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team that translating and checking written labels are among the first tasks AI will take. We should count wrong care instructions before management decides how many reviewers stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company might keep fewer people on each clothing line and combine managers. I’m experienced, but if the team is cut in half I could lose hours or the whole post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d test the translation tool on seventy old labels, including the raincoat error, and count every wrong fabric warning. In the first year I’d learn its review screen on paid time and take five paid hem-repair orders from neighbours only if Leo can cover the children while I sew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about being cut, but I can see a small second income I already know how to make. Five hems will not replace a manager wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge for a hem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d quote 12 for a simple trouser hem and write down the hours. If it takes me all evening, it is not a business yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell management about the paid hems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check the outside-work rule and tell them if it requires disclosure. Sewing is my own time, but I will not hide a conflict with the company.

say: I’d count **wrong fabric warnings** across our clothing lines before reducing label reviewers.
Translation and checking are **early exposed tasks**.
think: A smaller team could cut **my hours or post**.
Experience does not guarantee a job if **manager slots shrink**.
do: Test **seventy old labels** for wrong care instructions.
Learn the **review screen** on paid time.
Take five **paid hems** only with Leo’s childcare; check outside-work rules and disclose if required.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can test a small second income.
S1.quote: Five hems will not replace a manager wage.
fieldNote: She tests **fabric warnings**, not just fluent wording.
Her experienced standing does not erase **manager consolidation** risk.
Hem work is conditional on **Leo covering childcare** and real paid orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company to name who signs off a care label and when translation posts will close. Customers should know who answers when an AI instruction damages a coat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could translate and check every label better and cheaper than my team, so I expect my post to go. Alterations still need hands until robots arrive around 2031, but the few hems I can sew will not pay our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This weekend Leo and I would list the mortgage, food and school costs and stop the summer camp deposit. Before 2028 I’d ask two local alteration shops about paid vacancies and keep taking only orders that cover materials; in the first year after AGI, I’d take a posted shop job only if its written pay covers my share of the mortgage and the hours leave one parent home after school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. We have three weeks saved, and the idea of losing my wage before the next term makes my stomach tighten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop can offer only a few hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep sewing those hours if they pay, but I would still search for a full wage. I will not call a busy sewing machine a paid mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the camp decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our children that we are protecting the house while I look for work. I would ask Leo whether the older child could still attend the free local program.

say: I’d seek **label sign-off** and written closure dates before an automated rollout.
Customers need a **human damage contact** after AI errors.
think: Alterations may last until **2031 robots**, but small orders cannot cover the mortgage.
do: Stop the **summer camp deposit** after reviewing bills with Leo.
Ask **two shops** about vacancies; keep a few paid sewing hours while seeking a full wage.
Take a **posted shop job** after 2028 only if written wages cover my mortgage share and one parent is home after school.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the tiny reserve and lost wage.
S2.quote: I will not call a busy sewing machine a paid mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **thinking-heavy label work** faces 2028 AGI directly.
Alterations are a **short bridge** before 2031 robots.
A shop role requires **written wages** and childcare-compatible hours.

steps.text: Stop the summer camp deposit after reviewing mortgage and school costs with Leo
Ask two local alteration shops about paid vacancies before 2028
Accept posted shop work with written pay covering mortgage share and parent home after school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough to check every AI label against real products and to give reviewers honest notice. A company can plan that without pretending all jobs are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a small alterations book while our label desk still pays me. A tailor shop also has bookings and price quotes that AGI could handle in 2031, while the sewing itself faces robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d take ten paid repair orders only if Leo’s school hours let him handle our younger child after school, and I’d keep a ledger of materials and hours. Before 2031 I’d apply for a posted alterations-supervisor role only if its wage covers my mortgage share; after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while the shop pays for hands-on repair work, not for quotes a system can write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years lets me find out whether anyone will pay me for sewing. I would not borrow to buy machines before ten real orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise your price if the work took too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after I see the actual hours for each repair. I would rather refuse a job than ask Leo to cover every evening for pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a supervisor role is only paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it is no shelter from 2031 AGI. I would look for paid bench work, but only if the combined wages cover the mortgage.

say: I’d demand **honest written notice** for label reviewers before the desk shrinks.
The company should check AI labels against **real garments**.
think: Shop quotes face **2031 AGI** even if sewing continues.
I could build **paid repair orders** while the label desk still pays me.
do: Take **ten paid repairs** only with Leo’s childcare coverage.
Apply for **posted alterations work** only at mortgage-covering pay and real bench duties.

feel: I feel **anxious** but can count actual orders.
S3.quote: I would not borrow to buy machines before ten real orders.
fieldNote: She treats **paid orders** and recorded hours as proof of demand.
She sees a supervisor’s **quotes exposed** to 2031 AGI.

steps.text: Take ten paid alteration orders only if Leo covers after-school care
Record materials and hours for each paid repair
Apply for alterations work before 2031 only if pay covers mortgage share and duties include sewing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade gives the company time to show which label jobs end and to pay people for the work they still do. I would want written dates, not a launch-day surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036, and our younger child would be seventeen. If Leo and I keep our wages, we could finally build a reserve and pay down the mortgage, but label writing and shop bookings still face 2036 AGI; robots reach sewing around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 we’d transfer 90 monthly to savings only when Leo’s school-kitchen pay is full and the mortgage is current. I’d keep the label job while it exists, take paid repairs on Saturdays only if ten orders a month actually arrive, and apply for a posted shop role before 2036 only if its written wage covers the mortgage; after AGI, I’d stay only while the shop pays for human sewing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, though a decade makes it possible to build money behind us. I would rather own one small box of sewing tools than a big loan for a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you open your own alterations shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the accounts showed enough paying customers after materials and rent. I would not put our family house behind a sign on an empty street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger child about studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say learn a skill you enjoy and ask what jobs pay, because both screens and hands will change. I would not write their plans for them.

say: I’d ask for **written end dates** for label jobs.
Workers should be **paid for remaining work** during change.
think: I could build **savings** before age 53 if both wages hold.
Shop bookings face **2036 AGI** before 2039 sewing robots.
do: Save **90 monthly** only when Leo’s pay and mortgage are current.
Keep the **label job**; take paid Saturday repairs only with ten monthly orders, and seek a mortgage-covering shop offer.
Stay in **shop work** after 2036 only while human sewing remains paid.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can build a reserve.
S4.quote: I would not put our family house behind a sign on an empty street.
fieldNote: She refuses a shop lease without **paying customers** after costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the label desk could close before our three-week reserve grows. Written notice, a posted alterations role with a wage we can check and after-school coverage would help. Sewing is only a plan when someone pays for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who takes the blame when a translated care label ruins a customer’s coat. The customer wears the mistake long after our team closes the file.

headlineQuote: The customer wears the mistake long after our team closes the file.
portrait: **Lena**, 43, is an experienced clothing-label manager with a bachelor’s degree.
Lower pay and **three weeks saved** strain a mortgage and two school-age children.
She uses AI **occasionally**, after a colleague checks it on old labels.
She tests **paid alterations** against real orders while keeping Leo’s childcare and wages in view.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close the label desk before her small repair income grows.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a posted alterations wage and after-school coverage would support a move.
